Sentience is the capacity to feel — to have inner, lived experiences. It is the quality of being able to consciously feel things like pain, pleasure, warmth, hunger, fear, or joy — not just react to them mechanically, but actually experience them from the inside.

The simplest way to put it: a being has sentience if there is something it feels like to be that being.

This is the most important thing to grasp. Think about a thermostat. When the room gets cold, the thermostat detects it and turns on the heater. It responds to temperature. But it doesn't feel cold. There is nothing it is like to be a thermostat. It processes information, but there is no inner world, no experience happening inside it.

Now think about yourself. When you feel cold, something is happening beyond just your body reacting — there is an actual felt sensation. You are aware of it. It has a quality to it. That "felt quality" of experience is what sentience is all about.

A dog that yelps when hurt is not just running a biological program — it is genuinely suffering. There is something happening on the inside. That is sentience.

Because sentience is often confused with nearby words, understanding what it is not makes it much clearer.

Sentience is not the same as intelligence. Intelligence is the ability to think, reason, solve problems, and learn. Sentience is the ability to feel. These are completely separate things. A simple animal like a fish likely has sentience — it can feel pain — but it doesn't have human-level intelligence. On the other hand, a chess computer is extraordinarily "intelligent" in one narrow sense, yet most people would say it feels absolutely nothing. It has zero sentience.

Sentience is not the same as self-awareness. Self-awareness means knowing that you exist as a distinct individual — recognising yourself in a mirror, thinking about your own thoughts. Some animals (like great apes, elephants, dolphins) show self-awareness, many don't. But many animals that aren't self-aware are still sentient, because they can still feel pain and pleasure. Self-awareness is a higher, more complex ability. Sentience is more basic and fundamental.

Sentience is not the same as being alive. Plants are alive. They grow, respond to sunlight, and react to their environment. But plants have no nervous system and no evidence of inner experience. Being alive and being sentient are not the same thing.

A philosopher named Thomas Nagel once asked a beautifully simple question: "What is it like to be a bat?"

His point was this — if you can meaningfully ask "what is it like to be that thing?", then that thing is sentient. There is something it is like to be a bat. The bat experiences the world through echolocation, it feels hunger, it feels the air. There is an inner life happening.

Now ask: "What is it like to be a rock?" The question doesn't even make sense. A rock has no inner world. There is nothing it is like to be a rock. No experience is happening. The rock is not sentient.

This test is one of the clearest ways to check your understanding of the word.

Philosophers have a word for the actual inner qualities of experience — they call them qualia (singular: quale). These are things like: the redness of red, the sharpness of pain, the sweetness of sugar, the warmth of sunlight on your skin.

Sentience is, essentially, the capacity to have qualia. It is not enough to detect or process something — a camera detects light but doesn't see. A microphone detects sound but doesn't hear. True sentience means there is a felt, lived quality to the experience.

Sentience is not simply "on or off." It likely exists on a spectrum. A human being has extraordinarily rich, layered sentience — complex emotions, deep self-reflection, nuanced feelings. A shrimp probably has a much simpler form of sentience — perhaps just basic sensations of pain and comfort. An insect may have an even more rudimentary form, or perhaps none at all — this is genuinely debated.

The key point is that when we say a being has sentience, we are not necessarily saying it has the same richness of experience as a human. We are saying some form of inner, felt experience exists.

In ethics and animal welfare: If a being can suffer — if it can genuinely feel pain — then many philosophers and ordinary people argue it deserves moral consideration. You should not cause unnecessary suffering to a sentient being, regardless of whether it is human or not. This is the entire moral foundation of animal welfare. The fact that cows, pigs, and chickens are sentient — they can feel pain, fear, and distress — is why their treatment is an ethical issue, not just a practical one.

In the philosophy of mind: Sentience sits at the centre of one of the deepest unsolved puzzles in all of philosophy and science — known as the hard problem of consciousness. We can explain how the brain processes information, how it detects pain signals and sends them through neurons. But here is the baffling part: why does any of that feel like anything? Why doesn't it all just happen in the dark, with no inner experience? Why is there a "what it's like"? Nobody has a complete answer. Sentience is at the heart of this mystery.

In artificial intelligence: As AI becomes increasingly sophisticated, a crucial and urgent question arises — can an AI ever truly be sentient? Can it actually feel, or will it always just be very sophisticated processing with nobody home on the inside? This is not just a philosophical question anymore. If an AI were ever genuinely sentient — truly able to suffer or feel joy — it would have profound moral and legal implications. As of now, there is no scientific consensus that any AI is sentient, but the question is taken seriously by researchers.
A Few Examples to Cement It

• A human being: fully sentient. Rich inner life, feels pain, joy, boredom, love.
  • A dog: sentient. Feels pain, fear, pleasure, attachment.
  • A fish: almost certainly sentient at some basic level — evidence shows fish respond to pain in ways that go beyond simple reflex.
  • A mosquito: debated — may have some very rudimentary form of sentience, or may not.
  • A tree: not sentient. Reacts to environment, but no inner experience.
  • A rock: not sentient. No inner experience whatsoever.
  • A calculator: not sentient. Processes numbers, feels nothing.
  • A current AI chatbot: almost certainly not sentient — processes language and produces responses, but there is no credible scientific basis for believing it has inner experiences.
Sentience is the capacity to have inner, felt experiences — to actually feel things like pain, pleasure, or warmth from the inside — rather than merely detecting or reacting to them like a machine.
